newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan nuclear firm alienates allies with bungles.
newsitem.headline: Japan nuclear firm alienates allies with bungles.

text.p: Revelations about lax safeguards at the site of Japan's worst nuclear accident have set off calls for an overhaul of the state-run firm that runs the country's ambitious nuclear fuel reprocessing programme.

While Japan's tiny environmental movement has always been critical of the Power Reactor and Nuclear Fuel Development Corp (PNC), the firm's safety lapses have now made critics of even strong proponents of Tokyo's quest to master plutonium technology to boost its energy self-sufficiency.

"The PNC was overconfident about safety and unequipped to cope after the accident," said Seiroku Kajiyama, the top government spokesman, who hails from the region where the March 11 fire and explosion exposed 37 workers to radiation.
"In terms of hardware and software, the firm is riddled with shortcomings," he told a news conference on Monday.

The nuclear fallout from the Tokaimura nuclear reprocessing plant, 160 km (100 miles) northeast of Tokyo, was enough to rate a three -- "serious incident" -- on the International Nuclear Event Scale of seven.
But the public relations disaster has been worse for the PNC, already reeling from an accident and embarrassing cover-up attempt last year at the Monju fast-breeder reactor it runs in western Japan.

The fiasco comes at a time when respect for Japan's bureaucracy is at an all-time low and state-run firms face pressure to justify their existence or face privatisation or disbandment under Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's plan to trim bloated bureaucracies and cut state spending.

The drumbeat of calls for privatisation or disbandment of the 30-year-old PNC, which has a staff of 2,800 and a 1996 budget of $2 billion, has grown louder with each report of bureaucrat bungling and safety slackness.

Trade Minister Shinji Sato, whose ministry has a hand in the plutonium plans, called for a "rethinking of the way PNC works" and officials at the Science and Technology Agency have publicly criticised "arrogance" at the firm it oversees.

On Tuesday the beleaguered PNC gave its growing ranks of critics new material to tee off on when it admitted that in an act of "extremely imprudent behavior", seven maintenance workers went golfing the day of the accident and the following day.

The golf incident follows revelations that the firm failed to inform nearby residents of the accident and did not warn a group of 64 people touring the facility at the time of the fire or check them later for exposure to radiation.

The PNC's bungling has chastened private power companies, which have a long-term commitment to Japan's scheme to use plutonium reprocessing to boost the natural resource-poor country's energy self sufficiency to more than 50 percent by the early 21st century.

Since the Tokaimura incident, two other nuclear plants have either shut or cut back production because of maintenance checks that found flaws in their operations. Another has postponed a plan to expand its production.
The group which represents the private sector electric power industry acknowledges the public relations fiasco, but says it is too early to talk of dismantling the PNC.

"What is most important first is to determine the cause of the accident and take measures to prevent a reoccurence," said a spokesman for the Federation of Electric Power Companies, which represents nine regional power concerns.
Member firms operate 50 nuclear reactors in 17 commercial plants nationwide.

"There is clearly a lot of public criticism, but that does not change our view that the plutonium reprocessing programme is indispensible for the country in terms of energy security and the environment," the spokesman told Reuters.
